subject: This is regarding 1530 s main st
comment: I understand there's a council meeting regarding the location where the main street motel is located. I have lived here for 4 years now waiting for housing. Me and my boyfriend are on the waiting list for housing and have been for 3 years. I'm currently in the process of applying for SSD my boyfriend has an income. We pay 70 $ a day here. But we can't seem to find affordable housing. If you tare this motel down you will be putting 2 people for every room here on the streets. I just hope the city will find about 3 motels, if they dont I hope they tare down this motel without giving us low income people that have made this place our home only because we can't get affordable housing from the state we live in. Thank you for your time

subject: 2100 S reconstruction
comment: Hi Alejandro, I live in Glendale and wanted to contact you regarding the upcoming city decision on the reconstruction of 2100 S from 700 to 1300 E. While I, as a Westsider, primarily hope to see the city invest in connectivity across the I-15 and railroad corridor, I also feel that 2100 S can be hugely improved should the city choose to do so. I hope that you will plan to support the second option- 3 lanes with a bikeway- to improve the safety and accessibility of this stretch of road. I regularly visit the Sugarhouse neighborhood, and usually travel there by bike. While this is not a difficult ride, the hostile designs of roads like I-15, State St., and 2100 S complicate it. I myself was nearly struck catastrophically on 2100 S for reasons directly related to the current 4-lane design: while walking across the street, a car which had stopped for me in a left lane blocked the view of a car in the right lane, which did not slow down whatsoever. Had I not been paying close attention, this would have resulted in a collision with debilitating consequences if not worse. To me, this safety consideration is just one of several pitfalls of the 4-lane design, but I have not yet seen it mentioned. Like others who have spoken on this issue, I also strongly feel that bike infrastructure improvements and traffic calming will be beneficial to both neighborhood residents and local businesses. Thanks for your consideration! -Adam Cook

subject: RE: (EXTERNAL) 2100 South Updates
comment: Please consider adding protected bike lanes when this street is updated. There is so much potential for this street, but it currently serves nobody. It is too chaotic for cars, too dangerous for pedestrian traffic, and provides no safety for bike commuters. If people want to zoom down the street at high speeds, I think they should use I-15 nearby. Please consider the notion of wider sidewalks and a protected bike lane when this street is updated in 2024. Thank you for the forward-thinking positive changes we have seen in Sugarhouse

subject: RE: (EXTERNAL) Sugarhouse 2100 South Option 2
comment: I'm writing to express my support for option 2 for the rebuild of 2100 South, as discussed in this article from Sweet Streets: https://sweetstreetslc.org/news/its-time-to-create-a-main-street-for-sugar-house. I love walking through Sugar House, and think 2100 South has an amazing opportunity to be a pleasant main street with sidewalk cafes, bike lanes, and safe paths for pedestrians. Right now it's a noisy mess with way too much traffic, and it makes me nervous every time I try to cross the street. It has so much potential, and I would love to see it reach that potential! Sincerely, Dan Berger J.D.

subject: Sad News, Personal Grief & A Call to Action for Salt Lake's Planning & Design Community
comment: Friends, as I'm processing my personal grief and horror, I feel compelled to reach out to the professional planning and design community, community leaders and others that I have worked and associated with over the past 3 decades in Utah, both to share the grief I'm processing, but also to motivate a call to action. There was a tragic auto-pedestrian accident in my neighborhood on Wednesday as an 11-year-old girl was crossing 2100 East just crosswalk at a signalized intersection, on her walk home from school. This makes me so sad, but also very, very angry. My younger daughter, who is the same age, goes to school at the nearby Jr. High just a few blocks away, and the girl who was killed was in her circles of friends. Many of them were sharing their grief and anxiety behind the scenes at a holiday dance event they were performing at last evening. There was another accident two months ago on 2300 East, where a boy who goes to my daughter's school was hit in a school zone crosswalk on his way to school...fortunately this boy walked away. This hits particularly close to home because my oldest daughter, now 24, was hit while walking her bicycle across the street in yet another school zone crosswalk on 2100 East, which is the street we live on, almost a decade ago. I introduced this news while I was at an opening night event during the CNU 21 International urban design and placemaking conference being held in Salt Lake City in the spring of 2023. Ironically while we were advocating for safer streets for pedestrians and bicycles in Salt Lake City. The thing is, we have policies going back more than 30 years in every city and neighborhood plan in Salt Lake City that direct city officials and professional staff to PRIORITIZE pedestrians and bicycle safety and functions, while most transportation projects continue to prioritize cars. I can highlight with every city street and state highway project in the last decade completed in Salt Lake City, and every major project currently under construction and in design in Salt Lake City (in Sugar House, we have 900 East under construction, and 1300 East, Highland Drive/1100 East and 2100 South currently in design stages), many of which have and are thankfully incorporating more and better pedestrian and bicycle facilities than ever before, but still fall far, far short of PRIORITIZING pedestrians and bicycles over the convenience and movement of cars. Case in point: About 3 or 4 years ago the intersection at 21st South and 21st East was completely reconstructed while 2100 East was going through a major pavement reconstruction project. Both the Sugar House Master Plan adopted in 2001 and updated in 2005, and the 21st & 21st Small Area Plan adopted in 2017, direct the City to improve pedestrian and bicycle facilities generally, the latter with recommendations for this intersection specifically. No meaningful pedestrian or bicycle safety improvements were incorporated into this project. My younger daughter walked to school almost every day for the past 7 years to her elementary school on 2100 East (I walked with her most of those days until she was in the 6th grade and said she could do it without dad), across this major 2100 East intersection, and I have witnessed her and many kids of my neighbors experience minor hits and near misses at this intersection going to and coming home from school. Were it not for the "hell for drivers" crossing guard we have at this intersection for a half hour before and after school, shouting at the bad behaviors of drivers, I'm sure we would have many more serious or even fatal accidents here. A major redevelopment project is happening at this intersection right now, and at least one corner of the intersection will again be completely reconstructed, though I have little faith or evidence based on prior plans I've seen that any substantive improvements for pedestrians and bicycles will be added as a result of this project other than a new (fantastic, thank you) bus stop where Blue Plate Diner used to be. It's infuriating to hear how awful tragedies like this are, while we continue as a society and community to see many of the actions to prevent them not being taken. We need to be much better designers of our public realm. Design will not solve every problem, but design that is consistent with our priorities and adopted policies can and will prevent more of these kinds of tragedies. As an urban design community, in the position to plan, and even more important to design and implement the best communities we know humans are capable of creating, we can and must be much more vocal and outspoken advocates to create cities that are safe and that work for everyone, and especially for those who do not or cannot drive a car. Here are four organizations working at the forefront of safer streets, and I urge you to get involved with each and all of them: Strong Towns (they do not have a local chapter or affiliate) Sweet Streets SLC Congress for the New Urbanism (we need Utah's chapter reinvigorated) Urban Design Utah And to those who lead each of these organizations, let's find ways to do more together that any of us or our organizations can do on our own. In sadness and renewed action - Soren Simonsen

subject: RE: (EXTERNAL) 2100 South rebuild
comment: Hello council-member Fowler, I am writing to you to express my support for option 2 of the 2100 south redevelopment plan proposed by Salt Lake City transportation. As a resident of the Sugar House neighborhood, I can say having a walkable core district is of high importance for me. The defining feature of a good community and neighborhood is a walkable and pedestrian friendly space, something that sugarhouse is currently lacking. I would ask that you voice your support for option 2 and when you are able, vote for its approval. Thank you, Daniel Munger
